synopsis: The booklet uses wheeled versus crawler as the first discriminator for machine families with separate braking models, because their physics, brake standards and test methods differ; machine types and brake systems were not yet confirmed during the research [f13733, f5864]. ISO 3450:2011, confirmed in 2022, covers wheeled earth-moving machines and rubber-tracked machines with top speeds of at least 20 km/h, while ISO 10265:2008 covers crawlers at 20 km/h or less; the stated scopes therefore meet at exactly 20 km/h [f15190, f5979]. Tracks retain more shear force than tires in soft soil, and crawler modeling must account for distributed ground contact, sinkage, differential track speed, skid steering and counter-rotation; collisions can occur without longitudinal closing speed [f6007, f6023, f6024, f6218]. No universal safe deceleration was found across machine types, loads and slopes, so the proposed operating-domain taxonomy includes surface conditions, grade, cross-slope, tire or track state and payload [f6310, f6724]. A published 2026 tracked-vehicle electro-hydraulic brake response is under 0.3 seconds, and a single-machine hydraulic model reported pressure accuracy above 96% and response-time accuracy above 95%; these results are architecture-specific and do not establish temperature or wear effects [f5893, f13668, f6438, f13816]. Virtual validation has supporting tools and calibration examples: Chrono models wheeled and tracked vehicles on deformable terrain, while TERA compared track deformation and terrain-dependent velocity against a real excavator, with a December 2024 preprint and SIMPAR 2025 publication [f9333, f4130].
